text: Rana Ayyub, born on 1 May 1984 in Mumbai, India, is an Indian journalist and opinion columnist for The Washington Post. She is the author of the investigative book Gujarat Files: Anatomy of a Cover Up. Her father, Mohammad Ayyub Waqif, was a writer for Blitz, a Mumbai-based magazine, and a member of the progressive writers movement; her uncle, Abdul Haq Azmi, was a distinguished Hadith scholar and senior professor at Darul Uloom Deoband. Ayyub contracted polio at age five, which left her left hand and right leg immobile, but she eventually recovered. During the 1992–93 Mumbai riots, her father warned her that local men were targeting his daughters; at nine years old, Rana fled with her sister to stay with a Sikh friend’s relatives for three months before returning to Deonar, a Muslim-majority suburb, where she grew up. She is a practising Muslim and graduated in English literature from Sophia College, Mumbai, where she studied with Richa Chada and Shuchi Talati. At Tehelka, a Delhi-based investigative news magazine, Ayyub conducted an eight-month undercover sting operation posing as Maithili Tyagi, a student of the American Film Institute with ideological ties to the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh, to gather recordings from Gujarat bureaucrats and police officers regarding encounter killings and the aftermath of the 2002 Gujarat riots. The recordings, made using a concealed device, were documented in her book Gujarat Files. However, Tehelka’s management refused to publish any story based on the recordings, citing that the data was incomplete or of inadequate quality. Ayyub continued working with Tehelka for several months before resigning in November 2013 in protest against the handling of sexual harassment allegations against editor-in-chief Tarun Tejpal. She now works independently. In September 2019, The Washington Post nominated her as a Contributing Global Opinions Writer. In 2021, on HARDtalk, she explained her ability to critique the government due to Indian media censorship. In October 2020, she published an open letter in Inquilab: A Decade of Protest, protesting the appointment of Gajendra Chauhan as chairman of FTII. Historian Ramachandra Guha called Gujarat Files "a brave book," and several journalists have privately praised her courage. Nilanjan Mukhopadhyay noted the bravery required in conducting undercover interviews during the investigation. The investigation was listed by Outlook as one of the twenty greatest magazine stories of all time. In 2018, Ayyub was awarded "most Resilient Global journalist" by Free Press Unlimited for resisting attempts to silence her. In the Haren Pandya murder case, the Supreme Court dismissed her book, stating it was based on surmises and had no evidentiary value; Ayyub called the ruling "puzzling," noting the CBI had used her work as evidence and that no official had denied her claims. In 2019, she accompanied Dexter Filkins from The New Yorker on a trip to Kashmir to report on government violence following the revocation of Kashmir’s special status, highlighting torture of Kashmiri civilians, including minors, which contrasted with official claims. In February 2022, the Enforcement Directorate (ED) froze assets worth over ₹1.77 crore of hers in a money laundering case alleging she embezzled public funds raised for pandemic relief. The ITAT in Mumbai found that only 10 per cent of the relief funds were used for relief work, with the rest transferred to her father’s and sister’s accounts and then to her personal account. International observers have described the charges as sham, part of a broader campaign to intimidate her and silence her criticism of the Modi government. A FIR was filed against her in Dharwad for allegedly calling anti-hijab protestors Hindu terrorists. In 2022, UN experts urged India to stop judicial harassment against her, including repeated bank freezes, calling the fund allegations "bogus" and linked to a far-right social media group. Online abuse against Ayyub is primarily driven by Twitter users aligned with Hindu nationalism and the ruling BJP; an ICFJ report found that Twitter failed to address the abuse and withheld her tweets at the request of the Indian government, with abuse often arriving within 14 seconds of her posting. In 2018, she received multiple death and rape threats, her personal details were leaked, and a deepfake pornographic video was released; Delhi Police closed the case in August 2020 due to inability to identify the perpetrators. Several UN Special Rapporteurs have intervened three times, warning of a serious risk to her life and calling on Indian authorities to protect her. The U.S. State Department’s 2020 Human Rights Report specifically mentioned the online trolling and threats against her. Reporters Without Borders also documented the hate speech against her and called on the government and Delhi police to protect her. In 2022, Hindu nationalist alt-right groups created the app Bulli Bai, which falsely auctioned Muslim women, and the secret app Tek Fog, used by BJP supporters to spread right-wing propaganda, targeted Ayyub and other prominent women journalists. In November 2024, Ayyub was doxxed, with her phone number leaked by a right-wing account on X, resulting in hundreds of calls and messages, with no respite despite filing a police complaint. In November 2025, she received threats of violence against herself and her father from an unknown international number, which she claimed were intended to intimidate her into writing a column on the 1984 anti-Sikh riots following the assassination of Indira Gandhi.
